title: Camp 3 close: your week has a shape
hook: Shabbat, blessings, holidays, study: a life with rhythm

segments.voice: Yesterday, the blessing before study: be busy with the words of Torah. Your line was bless the words first. Today is the last day of this camp, so we look back at all of it. Day one hundred fifty-six.

Sixty days ago this camp began with a promise: I can do this. Not believe this. Do this. A candle, a cup, a blessing, a breath. Think about what most weeks look like. Monday blurs into Thursday. The weekend fills up with errands. Holidays sneak up and pass. It's a line with no shape, just more. Judaism answers that with rhythm. Every day has its words, every week has its peak, every year has its seasons. Today, before a new camp begins, we walk back through what you've practiced, and you choose what to keep.
screen: `I CAN DO THIS.` → `A WEEK WITH NO SHAPE.` → `A LIFE WITH RHYTHM.`

segments.voice: It started with Shabbat, holy time, not holy place. Erev Shabbat, getting ready as if a guest were coming. Candles, hands over the eyes. Kiddush over a cup. Two loaves of challah, covered. Melacha, the kinds of work set aside, and menuchah, real rest. The third meal at dusk, and Havdalah's braided candle and spices to carry the scent into the week. Then the blessings through the day. Modeh Ani, thank you before you get up. Baruch, the word that opens almost every blessing. Hamotzi over bread, Birkat Hamazon after the meal, Shehecheyanu for firsts, and even a blessing inside grief. Then the year. The luach, a calendar kept by the moon. The shofar's cry, the sukkah's leafy roof, Hanukkah's lights going up, the seder's questions, counting the Omer to Shavuot. Tefillin on arm and head. Kosher, which means fit. And this last week: Talmud Torah, study as worship. Chavruta, learning in pairs. The good question. Rashi on your shoulder. Machloket for heaven's sake. The blessing before study. Look at the shape all that makes. The Torah itself begins it: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Six days of work, then a day that's different. Three times a day, prayer. A hundred small blessings. Holidays that come back every year, so you meet yourself again. Nobody does all of it at once, and Jews keep these practices in very different ways. But a week can have a shape. The next camp opens the book at the center of it all: the Torah, one portion a week.
screen: `SHABBAT: CANDLES, CUP, TWO LOAVES.` · `BLESSINGS THROUGH THE DAY.` · `THE YEAR: SHOFAR TO SHAVUOT.` · `STUDY: PAIRS, QUESTIONS, RASHI.` · then, large: `THE WEEK HAS A SHAPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose three practices to keep. Settle, and breathe. Let the camp pass in front of you: the candle, the cup, thank you before you get up, the blessing after a meal, a question at dinner, a study partner. Which three felt like yours? Pick one for each day, one for each week, and one for the year. Hold them lightly. You can change them later. The bell holds the time.
Camp 3 close. Sixty days of practices: Shabbat, blessings, holidays, tefillin, kashrut and study, a week with a shape.
Your line: the week has a shape. Today, write down your three practices and put one on this week's calendar. Tomorrow, a new camp: the text, one portion a week. Day one hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Jews shape the week around Shabbat, the day around prayer and blessings, and the year around the festivals; how many of these practices a person keeps varies widely across communities and families.

original.note: Hebrew: a week, from the word for seven.

trapdoor: what you thought: religious practice is a long list of rules.
what it means: a rhythm: blessings through the day, Shabbat at the peak of the week, festivals around the year.
what a scholar hears: shavua, a week, from sheva, seven; Genesis 2:3 grounds the seven-day week in creation; Menachot 43b's hundred blessings a day.
